metadata.description: Scenario-Based Study Companion covering Google Cloud database and storage services including Cloud SQL, Cloud Spanner, Firestore, Bigtable, Cloud Storage, Filestore, Persistent Disk, and AlloyDB.

question.title: Cloud SQL Overview
question.scenario: A startup is migrating their existing MySQL application from on-premises to Google Cloud. They want a managed database solution that minimizes operational overhead while maintaining compatibility.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides fully managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server databases?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Which GCP database services are relational, and which of those support multiple popular open-source engines plus SQL Server out of the box?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud SQL is Google Cloud's fully managed relational database service supporting MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server. It automates backups, replication, patching, and capacity management. For a MySQL migration, Cloud SQL offers drop-in compatibility so existing application code requires minimal changes. Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store, Cloud Spanner targets global-scale relational needs at much higher cost, and AlloyDB is PostgreSQL-only with enhanced analytics performance.

ul.li: Cloud SQL instances scale up to 96 vCPUs, 624 GB RAM, and 64 TB storage, covering most traditional relational workloads without re-architecture.
Automatic storage increase can be enabled so the instance grows its disk on demand, preventing out-of-space failures during traffic spikes.
Cloud SQL supports Private IP via VPC peering and the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy for secure, certificate-free connectivity from GKE or Compute Engine.
Bigtable is NoSQL (no SQL joins or ACID transactions), Spanner is for global distribution at premium cost, and AlloyDB serves only PostgreSQL workloads.

question.title: Cloud SQL High Availability
question.scenario: An e-commerce company requires their Cloud SQL database to survive a zonal failure without manual intervention or data loss.
question.question-text: Which Cloud SQL configuration provides automatic failover to a standby instance in a different zone?

choices.choice: High availability configuration with regional instance

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the configuration that places a synchronous standby in a separate zone and triggers automatic failover when the primary becomes unreachable.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud SQL high availability (HA) creates a primary and a standby instance in different zones of the same region with synchronous replication. If the primary goes down, automatic failover promotes the standby with near-zero data loss. Read replicas use asynchronous replication designed for read scaling, not failover. External replicas are for migration or hybrid scenarios. Point-in-time recovery restores from backups but does not provide automatic failover.

ul.li: HA roughly doubles the instance cost because both primary and standby consume identical compute and storage resources continuously.
Failover typically completes in under 120 seconds; applications should use connection retry logic and exponential backoff to handle the brief interruption.
Read replicas can be promoted to standalone instances for disaster recovery, but this is a manual process and involves asynchronous lag, so some data loss is possible.
HA can be enabled or disabled on an existing instance without recreating it, though toggling triggers a brief restart.

question.title: Cloud Spanner Use Case
question.scenario: A global financial services company needs a relational database that provides strong consistency across multiple continents while supporting SQL queries and horizontal scaling.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud database is designed for global-scale relational workloads with strong consistency?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider the only GCP relational database that combines horizontal scaling across regions with externally consistent ACID transactions and full SQL support.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner is Google Cloud's globally distributed relational database offering strong (external) consistency, SQL support, schemas, and ACID transactions that scale horizontally. It is purpose-built for workloads like financial ledgers, inventory systems, and gaming backends that must serve users on multiple continents without sacrificing consistency. Cloud SQL is regional only, Firestore is a document-based NoSQL database, and BigQuery is an analytics data warehouse not designed for OLTP workloads.

ul.li: Spanner uses Google's TrueTime API — atomic clocks and GPS receivers in every data center — to achieve external consistency, meaning transactions have globally meaningful commit timestamps.
Minimum billing is one processing unit (or one node at roughly 1,000 processing units), with each node providing approximately 10,000 reads/sec or 2,000 writes/sec and up to 2 TB of storage.
Cloud SQL caps at a single region and a single write primary; Spanner's multi-region configurations distribute writes globally with automatic sharding.
Firestore provides strong consistency for individual document reads but is not a relational database and lacks SQL joins; BigQuery is optimized for batch analytics, not transactional reads/writes.

question.title: Cloud Spanner Configuration
question.scenario: A company is deploying Cloud Spanner for their globally distributed inventory system. They need to decide between regional and multi-region configurations.
question.question-text: What is the primary benefit of a Cloud Spanner multi-region configuration over a regional configuration?

choices.choice: Lower latency for all read operations
Higher availability SLA and survives regional outages

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Multi-region Spanner replicates data across multiple regions, offering a 99.999% SLA versus 99.99% for regional — focus on the availability and fault-tolerance benefit.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner multi-region configurations replicate data across several regions, delivering a 99.999% (five nines) availability SLA and the ability to survive an entire regional outage without data loss. Regional configurations offer 99.99% availability at lower cost but cannot tolerate a full region failure. Multi-region does not simplify schema design or reduce cost; in fact it costs roughly 3x more. Read latency for stale reads can improve via local replicas, but write latency increases due to cross-region consensus.

ul.li: Multi-region write latency is higher because Spanner must achieve quorum across geographically distant replicas before committing a transaction.
Stale reads (bounded staleness or exact staleness) can be served from the nearest replica, reducing read latency, but strong reads still route to the leader region.
Multi-region configurations cost approximately 3x a comparable single-region setup due to the extra replica storage and cross-region network traffic.
Google offers predefined multi-region configurations (e.g., nam-eur-asia1) and allows custom placements for specific compliance or latency requirements.

question.title: AlloyDB Introduction
question.scenario: A company running analytics-heavy PostgreSQL workloads needs better performance than Cloud SQL provides, while maintaining full PostgreSQL compatibility.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud database service offers PostgreSQL compatibility with up to 4x faster transactional workloads and 100x faster analytical queries?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the fully managed GCP database that pairs full PostgreSQL wire compatibility with Google-proprietary storage and an integrated columnar analytics engine.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a fully managed, PostgreSQL-compatible database built on Google's proprietary storage and compute infrastructure. It delivers up to 4x faster transactional throughput and 100x faster analytical queries compared to standard PostgreSQL, with a 99.99% availability SLA that includes maintenance windows. Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL uses standard PostgreSQL without the columnar engine. Cloud Spanner's PostgreSQL interface has dialect limitations and is not fully compatible. BigQuery is a data warehouse, not a transactional database.

ul.li: AlloyDB separates compute from a log-structured distributed storage layer, enabling read pool instances and the primary to scale independently without duplicating data.
The built-in columnar engine automatically materializes frequently queried columns in a columnar format, accelerating analytics without requiring ETL pipelines or separate data copies.
An ML-based adaptive system continuously optimizes vacuum scheduling, buffer pool management, and storage compaction based on observed workload patterns.
Cloud Spanner's PostgreSQL interface supports a subset of PostgreSQL syntax and lacks extensions, stored procedures, and full PL/pgSQL support that AlloyDB provides natively.

question.title: AlloyDB Architecture
question.scenario: An architect is designing a system using AlloyDB and needs to understand how to scale read capacity independently from the primary instance.
question.question-text: How does AlloyDB enable scaling read capacity without affecting the primary instance?

choices.choice: Cross-region read replicas with separate storage
Read pool instances that share storage with the primary
Automatic read query routing to BigQuery

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: AlloyDB's disaggregated architecture means read pool nodes connect to the same distributed storage layer as the primary, so adding read capacity requires no data duplication.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: AlloyDB separates compute from storage. Read pool instances are additional compute nodes that share the same distributed storage layer as the primary, so they see the latest committed data without asynchronous replication lag or storage duplication. This lets you spin up or tear down read capacity in minutes. Memory-only caching would lose data on restart, cross-region replicas with separate storage introduce replication lag and double storage cost, and routing to BigQuery adds latency and is not suitable for OLTP reads.

ul.li: Read pool instances can be provisioned or removed in minutes because they attach to existing storage rather than copying data, eliminating the bootstrap time of traditional replicas.
The shared storage layer replicates data synchronously across zones for durability, so all read pool nodes inherit the same regional resilience as the primary.
Applications connect to a single read pool endpoint that load-balances across all read pool nodes, simplifying connection management and avoiding application-side routing logic.
Unlike Cloud SQL read replicas, AlloyDB read pool instances do not maintain a separate WAL stream, reducing network overhead and ensuring near-zero read lag.

question.title: Database Migration Service
question.scenario: A company needs to migrate their on-premises Oracle database to Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with minimal downtime.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service facilitates database migrations to Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, or Cloud Spanner?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Focus on the serverless GCP service specifically designed for minimal-downtime database migrations, supporting both homogeneous and heterogeneous source-to-target paths.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Database Migration Service (DMS) is a fully managed, serverless service for migrating databases to Google Cloud targets including Cloud SQL, AlloyDB, and Cloud Spanner. It supports homogeneous migrations (e.g., MySQL to Cloud SQL MySQL) and heterogeneous migrations (e.g., Oracle to PostgreSQL) using continuous change data capture for minimal-downtime cutover. Transfer Appliance is for physical shipment of large datasets, Storage Transfer Service moves object storage data between providers, and Dataflow is a stream/batch processing engine — none are purpose-built for database schema and data migration.

ul.li: DMS uses change data capture (CDC) to continuously replicate changes from the source during migration, keeping the target in sync until cutover so downtime is limited to the switchover window.
For heterogeneous migrations, DMS integrates with schema conversion tools (e.g., Ora2Pg, the migration workspace) that translate source DDL, stored procedures, and data types to the target dialect.
Transfer Appliance ships physical storage devices for offline data movement; Storage Transfer Service operates on object/blob storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS), not relational databases.
DMS migration jobs are serverless — Google provisions and manages the replication infrastructure, and you pay only for the duration of active migration.

question.title: Cloud SQL Connection Methods
question.scenario: A developer needs to connect their application running on Google Kubernetes Engine to a Cloud SQL instance securely without managing SSL certificates.
question.question-text: What is the recommended method for connecting GKE workloads to Cloud SQL securely?

choices.choice: SSH tunnel through a bastion host

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider the lightweight proxy that handles IAM-based authentication and TLS encryption to Cloud SQL automatically, eliminating the need to manage SSL certificates or IP allowlists.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is Google's recommended connector for GKE-to-Cloud SQL communication. It runs as a sidecar container in each pod, uses IAM credentials for authentication, and encrypts the connection with TLS — all without requiring you to manage certificates, configure authorized networks, or expose a public IP. Direct VPC TCP connections are possible with Private IP but require VPC peering setup. Public IP with firewall rules is less secure and harder to maintain. SSH tunnels add operational overhead and latency.

ul.li: The Auth Proxy supports IAM database authentication, which maps IAM principals to database users, enabling centralized access control and eliminating the need for static database passwords.
In GKE, the proxy is typically deployed as a sidecar container that listens on localhost, so the application connects to 127.0.0.1 on the configured port and the proxy handles all upstream security.
Private IP connections via VPC peering are also secure and avoid the public internet, but they require VPC network configuration and do not provide IAM-based per-user authentication by default.
Public IP access requires maintaining authorized network CIDR ranges and rotating SSL certificates, making it operationally expensive compared to the Auth Proxy's automatic handling.

question.title: Cloud SQL Read Replicas
question.scenario: An application has high read traffic that overwhelms the primary Cloud SQL instance. The team wants to distribute read load while keeping the primary for writes.
question.question-text: Which Cloud SQL feature allows distributing read traffic across multiple instances?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the Cloud SQL feature that creates asynchronous copies of the primary instance specifically to offload read queries and scale read throughput horizontally.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud SQL read replicas are asynchronous copies of the primary that handle read queries, distributing read traffic and reducing load on the primary. Applications must direct reads to replica endpoints and writes to the primary. Query insights is a monitoring tool, not a scaling feature. HA configuration provides failover redundancy but does not serve read traffic. Connection pooling helps manage connection counts but does not add read capacity.

ul.li: Cloud SQL supports up to 10 read replicas per primary instance, and replicas can be placed in different zones or even cross-region for lower read latency in other geographies.
Replication is asynchronous, so replicas may lag the primary by seconds under heavy write load; applications must tolerate eventual consistency for replica reads.
Cross-region read replicas can be promoted to standalone primary instances for disaster recovery, though promotion severs the replication link permanently.
Read replicas do not participate in HA failover — they are separate from the HA standby instance and serve a different purpose (read scaling vs. write availability).

question.title: Cloud Spanner Schema Design
question.scenario: A team designing a Cloud Spanner schema for an order management system needs to store orders and order items. They want to optimize for queries that fetch an order with all its items.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Spanner schema design pattern optimizes parent-child data retrieval?

choices.choice: Separate tables with foreign key joins
Denormalized single table with repeated fields

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Spanner has a unique schema feature that physically co-locates child rows with their parent row on the same split, making parent-child reads a single local operation.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner's interleaved tables store child rows physically adjacent to their parent row within the same storage split. For an order management system, interleaving OrderItems under Orders means fetching an order and all its items reads contiguous storage, minimizing the number of splits accessed and reducing latency. Foreign key joins across non-interleaved tables may span multiple splits, increasing latency. Denormalization wastes storage and complicates updates. Spanner does not support cross-database queries.

ul.li: Interleaving is declared with the INTERLEAVE IN PARENT clause in DDL; child rows must include the parent's primary key columns as a prefix of their own primary key.
Interleaved tables share the same split as their parent, so a single read or transaction on a parent key range accesses all related child rows without cross-split coordination.

Avoid interleaving when parent-child data is rarely queried together or when child tables are very large, because co-location increases the size of individual splits and may trigger more frequent split operations.
ON DELETE CASCADE can be specified on interleaved tables so that deleting a parent row automatically removes all interleaved child rows in the same transaction.

question.title: Firestore Overview
question.scenario: A mobile app development team needs a database that automatically syncs data between the app and the cloud, supports offline access, and scales automatically.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud database provides real-time synchronization, offline support, and automatic scaling for mobile and web applications?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider the serverless NoSQL document database with built-in mobile/web SDKs that handle real-time listeners, offline caching, and automatic scaling to zero.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firestore is a serverless NoSQL document database that provides real-time listeners for instant data synchronization across devices, offline persistence so apps work without connectivity, and automatic scaling from zero to millions of users. It organizes data in documents and collections and supports multi-document ACID transactions. Cloud SQL is relational and requires provisioned instances, Bigtable is a wide-column store for analytics-scale workloads, and Memorystore is an in-memory cache without persistence or sync features.

ul.li: Firestore offers two modes: Native mode (full feature set including real-time listeners, offline persistence, and mobile SDKs) and Datastore mode (backward-compatible API for legacy Cloud Datastore applications).
Real-time listeners use a snapshot listener pattern that pushes incremental changes to connected clients, avoiding polling and minimizing bandwidth usage.
Pricing is based on document reads, writes, and deletes plus storage, making it cost-effective for low-traffic apps because there is no minimum provisioned capacity.
Firestore's offline cache persists data locally on the device, queues writes while offline, and automatically reconciles with the server when connectivity returns.

question.title: Firestore Modes
question.scenario: A team is migrating from Datastore to Firestore and needs to understand the differences between Firestore modes.
question.question-text: What is the main difference between Firestore Native mode and Datastore mode?

choices.choice: Datastore mode has higher query throughput than Native mode
Datastore mode supports SQL queries; Native mode does not
Native mode is regional only; Datastore mode is multi-regional
Native mode supports real-time updates and mobile SDKs; Datastore mode is compatible with legacy Datastore APIs

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The key distinction is feature set: Native mode unlocks real-time listeners and mobile/web SDKs, while Datastore mode preserves backward compatibility with the legacy Cloud Datastore API.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firestore Native mode delivers the full Firestore experience — real-time listeners, offline persistence, mobile and web SDKs, and the document/collection data model. Datastore mode maintains backward compatibility with Cloud Datastore APIs and client libraries, making it the right choice only when an existing Datastore application must migrate without rewriting data-access code. Neither mode supports SQL; both support strong consistency. Throughput and regional/multi-regional availability are configuration choices, not mode differences.

ul.li: Mode selection is permanent and cannot be changed after the database is created, so the decision must be made during initial provisioning.
Both modes now provide strong consistency for all queries, unlike the original Cloud Datastore which had eventual consistency for non-ancestor queries.
Native mode is recommended for all new applications; Datastore mode should only be chosen when maintaining compatibility with existing Datastore client libraries is a hard requirement.
Datastore mode does not support real-time listeners, mobile/web SDKs, or the collection-group query feature available in Native mode.

question.title: Firestore Security Rules
question.scenario: A web application uses Firestore directly from the browser. The team needs to ensure users can only read and write their own data.
question.question-text: What mechanism controls data access when clients connect directly to Firestore?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Direct client-to-Firestore access is governed by a declarative rules language evaluated server-side, not by IAM policies or network-layer controls.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firestore Security Rules are a server-side, declarative rules language that controls read and write access for mobile and web clients connecting directly to Firestore. Rules can reference the authenticated user's identity (via Firebase Authentication), inspect document fields, and validate incoming data shapes and values. Cloud IAM policies govern server-side (admin SDK) access, not client-side. VPC Service Controls and network firewall rules operate at the network perimeter and cannot enforce per-user, per-document authorization.

ul.li: Security Rules are evaluated entirely on Google's servers before any read or write is executed, so malicious clients cannot bypass them regardless of client-side code modifications.
Rules support custom functions for reusable validation logic, such as checking whether a user belongs to an organization or whether a field value falls within an allowed range.
The Firestore emulator allows local testing of Security Rules with unit tests before deploying to production, catching authorization bugs early in development.

IAM roles like roles/datastore.user control server-to-server access (e.g., from Cloud Functions), while Security Rules control end-user client access — both layers should be configured for defense in depth.

question.title: Bigtable Use Case
question.scenario: An IoT platform needs to store billions of time-series sensor readings with consistent low-latency access for both writes and reads.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud database is optimized for high-throughput, low-latency workloads with petabytes of data?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the wide-column NoSQL database that powers some of Google's own largest services and is designed for consistent sub-10ms latency at petabyte scale.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Bigtable is a fully managed, wide-column NoSQL database built for massive analytical and operational workloads. It delivers consistent single-digit millisecond latency for both reads and writes, handles petabytes of data, and scales throughput linearly by adding nodes. It is the ideal choice for time-series, IoT telemetry, and financial tick data. Firestore targets mobile/web document workloads, Cloud SQL is a relational database with single-instance scaling limits, and Cloud Spanner serves relational workloads needing global consistency rather than raw throughput at minimal latency.

ul.li: Bigtable is the same technology underlying Google Search, Maps, and Gmail, battle-tested at Google's own production scale for over a decade.
It exposes an Apache HBase-compatible API, so existing HBase applications can migrate with minimal code changes, and it integrates natively with Hadoop, Dataflow, and Dataproc.
Performance scales linearly: each node adds roughly 10,000 rows/sec throughput for reads or writes, and a cluster requires a minimum of one node.

Bigtable supports only single-row transactions and does not offer SQL or multi-row ACID guarantees, so workloads needing relational joins or cross-row atomicity should use Spanner or Cloud SQL instead.

question.title: Bigtable Row Key Design
question.scenario: A team is designing a Bigtable schema for storing user activity logs. They need to efficiently query recent activities for a specific user.
question.question-text: What is the recommended row key design for querying user activities by recency?

choices.choice: User ID combined with reverse timestamp

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: An effective Bigtable row key for this pattern prefixes with the user identifier to group data, then appends a reverse timestamp so the most recent entries sort first in a scan.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Combining user ID with a reverse timestamp (Long.MAX_VALUE minus the actual timestamp) as the row key groups all of a user's activities together in Bigtable's lexicographically sorted key space and ensures the most recent entries appear first in a row range scan. Timestamp-only keys create write hotspots on a single node. Auto-incrementing IDs cause the same hotspot problem. Random UUIDs distribute writes evenly but make per-user queries impossible without a full table scan.

ul.li: Monotonically increasing keys (plain timestamps, sequential IDs) concentrate all writes on one tablet server, creating a hotspot that limits throughput to a single node's capacity.
Row key design should reflect the most common access pattern: if queries always filter by user then sort by time, the key should encode that hierarchy (user first, time second).
Field promotion — adding query-predicate fields into the row key — is a core Bigtable design principle because Bigtable has no secondary indexes; all efficient lookups must be row key prefix scans.
For high-cardinality users, the user ID prefix naturally distributes writes across tablets; for low-cardinality groupings, consider salting the key with a hash prefix to avoid hotspots.

question.title: Bigtable Cluster Configuration
question.scenario: A company needs Bigtable to serve traffic from multiple regions with high availability and the ability to survive a regional outage.
question.question-text: How should Bigtable be configured for multi-region high availability?

choices.choice: Create a Bigtable instance with clusters in multiple regions using replication
Deploy separate Bigtable instances and sync data with Dataflow
Use Cloud Spanner instead as Bigtable does not support multi-region
Configure cross-region backup and restore procedures

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Bigtable natively supports multi-cluster replication within a single instance, automatically syncing data between clusters placed in different regions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Bigtable supports adding multiple clusters to a single instance, with each cluster in a different region. Replication between clusters is automatic and eventually consistent, typically converging within seconds. Applications can use app profiles to route traffic to the nearest cluster or fail over transparently during regional outages. Deploying separate instances with Dataflow sync is complex and fragile. Spanner is a different product for different workloads. Cross-region backup/restore has high RPO and does not provide continuous availability.

ul.li: Replication is eventually consistent with typical convergence lag under one minute; last-writer-wins conflict resolution applies when the same cell is written concurrently in different clusters.

App profiles control routing: multi-cluster routing sends traffic to the nearest healthy cluster, single-cluster routing pins to one cluster, and cluster group routing limits traffic to a subset of clusters.
Each cluster is billed independently for its node-hours and storage; inter-cluster replication network traffic is also billed, so multi-region costs scale with both cluster count and write volume.
You can add or remove clusters from a running instance without downtime; Bigtable automatically rebalances data to new clusters and drains removed clusters gracefully.

question.title: Bigtable vs Firestore
question.scenario: A team is choosing between Bigtable and Firestore for a new application that will store structured data with moderate query complexity.
question.question-text: When should you choose Firestore over Bigtable?

choices.choice: When you need document queries, real-time sync, and automatic scaling from zero
When you need to store petabytes of time-series data
When you need HBase API compatibility
When consistent sub-10ms latency is critical

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Firestore is the right pick when you need flexible document queries, real-time synchronization, mobile/web SDKs, and the ability to scale to zero during idle periods.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Choose Firestore when your application needs flexible document-model queries, real-time synchronization across clients, offline support, and serverless scaling that includes scaling to zero cost during inactivity. Choose Bigtable for analytics-scale workloads: petabytes of time-series or event data, consistent sub-10ms latency at high throughput, and HBase API compatibility. Bigtable requires at least one always-on node, making it cost-prohibitive for low-traffic or bursty apps where Firestore's pay-per-operation model excels.

ul.li: Firestore charges per document operation (read, write, delete) plus storage, so idle apps pay nearly nothing; Bigtable charges per node-hour with a minimum of one node regardless of traffic.
Bigtable supports only single-row transactions with no secondary indexes, while Firestore supports multi-document ACID transactions and automatic single-field indexes with optional composite indexes.
Firestore provides real-time listeners and offline persistence through client SDKs; Bigtable has no built-in sync or offline capability and is accessed via server-side HBase or gRPC APIs.

For workloads between 1 TB and 10 TB with moderate query complexity, the decision often hinges on access pattern: document lookups with real-time sync favor Firestore, while sequential scan and time-range queries favor Bigtable.

question.title: Memorystore Overview
question.scenario: An application needs to cache frequently accessed data to reduce database load and improve response times.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides managed Redis and Memcached for in-memory caching?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the fully managed GCP service that provides in-memory data stores using Redis or Memcached engines for sub-millisecond data access.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Memorystore is Google Cloud's fully managed in-memory data store service supporting both Redis and Memcached engines. It is designed for application caching, session management, leaderboards, and real-time analytics that require sub-millisecond read latency. Bigtable is a disk-based NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond latency. Cloud CDN caches HTTP responses at network edge locations, not application-level data. Firestore is a persistent document database, not an in-memory cache.

ul.li: Memorystore for Redis offers Basic tier (single node, no replication) and Standard tier (automatic failover with a replica in another zone for high availability).
Redis Cluster mode enables horizontal scaling beyond single-instance memory limits by sharding data across multiple nodes, supporting up to 300 GB per cluster.
Cloud CDN caches HTTP responses at Google's global edge points of presence; Memorystore caches arbitrary application data (objects, query results, session state) within a VPC network.
Memorystore for Redis supports RDB snapshots and AOF persistence for durability, but its primary value is speed — data should be reproducible from the source of truth if the cache is lost.

question.title: Firestore Indexes
question.scenario: A developer receives an error when running a Firestore query that filters on multiple fields.
question.question-text: Why might a Firestore query with multiple field filters fail?

choices.choice: Authentication is required for multi-field queries
Firestore does not support queries with multiple filters
A composite index must be created for queries with multiple field filters
The fields must be in the same document collection

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Firestore automatically indexes each field individually, but queries filtering on multiple fields require an explicitly created composite index covering those fields.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firestore creates single-field indexes automatically for every field in every document, but queries that filter or sort on multiple fields require a composite index that must be created explicitly. When a query needs a missing composite index, Firestore returns an error message that includes a direct link to the Cloud Console to create the required index. Authentication is not related to index availability, Firestore does support multi-field queries (with the right index), and fields must be in the queried collection but that is not the cause of the error.

ul.li: Composite indexes can be created via the Firebase Console, the gcloud CLI, or declaratively in a firestore.indexes.json file deployed with firebase deploy --only firestore:indexes.

Each composite index incurs storage overhead and adds write latency because Firestore must update the index entry on every write to an indexed field; limit composite indexes to queries you actually run.
Firestore enforces a maximum of 200 composite indexes per database; exceeding this limit requires consolidating query patterns or restructuring the data model.
Collection-group queries (querying across all subcollections with the same name) also require a composite index with collection-group scope, which must be enabled explicitly.

question.title: Bigtable Garbage Collection
question.scenario: A team stores time-series data in Bigtable and needs to automatically delete data older than 30 days to control costs.
question.question-text: How can Bigtable automatically remove old data based on age?

choices.choice: Create a separate table for each day and drop old tables
Schedule Cloud Functions to delete old rows
Configure garbage collection policies on column families
Use TTL settings on individual cells

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Bigtable uses garbage collection (GC) policies defined at the column family level to automatically expire cells by age or version count during background compaction.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Bigtable garbage collection policies are configured per column family and define when individual cells become eligible for automatic deletion. Policies can be based on cell age (e.g., delete cells older than 30 days) or version count (e.g., keep only the latest 3 versions). GC runs during background compaction, so expired data is removed without manual intervention. Creating separate tables per day is operationally complex, Cloud Functions introduce external scheduling overhead, and Bigtable does not support per-cell TTL settings independent of column family GC policies.

ul.li: GC policies can combine age and version rules using union (delete if either condition is met) or intersection (delete only if both conditions are met) logic for fine-grained retention control.
Expired data may still be returned by reads until the next compaction physically removes the cells; applications should not rely on GC for immediate deletion guarantees.
GC operates at the cell level, not the row level — removing all cells from a row does not delete the row key itself until compaction cleans up the empty row marker.
Different column families within the same table can have different GC policies, allowing hot data (recent metrics) and cold data (historical summaries) to coexist with independent retention rules.

question.title: Cloud Storage Overview
question.scenario: A media company needs to store large video files that will be accessed from applications worldwide.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides highly durable object storage for unstructured data?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider Google Cloud's object storage service that stores unlimited unstructured data in buckets with 11 nines of annual durability and global accessibility.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Storage is Google Cloud's globally available object storage service that stores data as immutable objects in buckets. It provides 99.999999999% (11 nines) annual durability, integrates with Cloud CDN for worldwide low-latency delivery, and supports multiple storage classes for cost optimization. Persistent Disk is block storage attached to VMs, Filestore provides NFS file shares, and Cloud SQL is a relational database — none are designed for large-scale unstructured data like video files.

ul.li: Individual objects can be up to 5 TB and there is no limit on the number of objects in a bucket or the total bucket size, making it suitable for media libraries of any scale.
Cloud Storage uses a flat namespace with object keys that can include slashes to simulate directory structures, but it is not a hierarchical file system — operations like rename are copy-then-delete.

Persistent Disk provides block storage for VM boot and data disks; Filestore provides POSIX-compliant NFS shares for multi-VM access; neither offers the global HTTP accessibility or CDN integration that Cloud Storage provides.
Cloud Storage supports parallel composite uploads and resumable uploads for large objects, enabling reliable transfer of multi-gigabyte video files over unreliable networks.

question.title: Cloud Storage Classes
question.scenario: A healthcare company must retain medical records for 7 years but will rarely access them after the first year.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Storage class offers the lowest storage cost for data accessed less than once a year?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The storage class with the lowest per-GB storage cost is designed for data accessed less than once a year, with a 365-day minimum storage duration and higher retrieval fees.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Storage Archive class has the lowest storage cost of all four classes, purpose-built for data accessed less than once per year. It carries the highest per-operation retrieval cost and a 365-day minimum storage duration charge. For a 7-year retention scenario with rare access, Archive minimizes total cost. Standard is for frequently accessed data, Nearline for monthly access (30-day minimum), and Coldline for quarterly access (90-day minimum). All four classes share identical 11-nines durability and millisecond first-byte latency.

ul.li: Storage cost ranking from highest to lowest: Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive; retrieval cost ranking is the inverse, with Archive being the most expensive to read.
All storage classes deliver the same 99.999999999% annual durability and millisecond-level access latency — the classes differ only in pricing structure and minimum storage duration.

Minimum storage durations — Nearline: 30 days, Coldline: 90 days, Archive: 365 days — mean deleting or overwriting an object before the minimum incurs an early-deletion charge equal to storing it for the full period.
Autoclass automatically transitions objects between Standard, Nearline, Coldline, and Archive based on access patterns, which can be useful when access frequency is unpredictable.

question.title: Object Lifecycle Management
question.scenario: A company wants to automatically move objects to cheaper storage classes as they age and delete them after 5 years.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Storage feature automates transitioning objects between storage classes?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The feature you need lets you define condition-action rules on a bucket that automatically transition objects to cheaper classes or delete them based on age, creation date, or other criteria.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Object Lifecycle Management lets you define rules on a bucket that automatically perform actions when objects meet specified conditions. Actions include SetStorageClass (transition to a cheaper class) and Delete (remove the object). Conditions include object age, creation date, current storage class, and version status. Rules are evaluated daily and applied asynchronously. Transfer Service moves data between locations, Object Versioning preserves previous versions, and Retention Policies prevent early deletion — none automate class transitions or scheduled deletion.

ul.li: Lifecycle rules support conditions including age, createdBefore, matchesStorageClass, numNewerVersions, isLive, and daysSinceCustomTime, enabling precise targeting of objects.
The SetStorageClass action can only transition to a colder class (Standard to Nearline to Coldline to Archive); you cannot use lifecycle rules to move objects to a warmer class.
The AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload action cleans up orphaned multipart upload fragments, preventing storage cost leaks from abandoned large-file uploads.
Retention policies and lifecycle Delete rules can conflict: a retention policy prevents deletion until the retention period expires, overriding any lifecycle Delete rule that would trigger earlier.

question.title: Cloud Storage Access Control
question.scenario: A company needs to provide temporary access to specific objects in Cloud Storage to external partners without creating Google accounts for them.
question.question-text: Which method provides time-limited access to Cloud Storage objects without requiring authentication?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Signed URLs provide time-limited, per-object access by embedding a cryptographic signature in the URL itself. Anyone with the URL can perform the allowed operation (read or write) until it expires, without needing a Google account or any authentication. VPC Service Controls restrict network-level access perimeters. IAM policies require Google identities. ACLs also require Google identities and do not support time-limited access. Only Signed URLs meet the requirement of temporary access for unauthenticated external partners.

ul.li: Signed URLs are generated using a service account's private key or HMAC keys, and the maximum expiration is 7 days when signing with service account credentials via the signBlob API.
Each Signed URL grants access to exactly one object and one HTTP method (GET, PUT, DELETE); separate URLs are needed for different objects or operations.
Signed Policy Documents extend the concept to uploads, allowing you to constrain the uploaded object's size, content type, and key prefix while still permitting unauthenticated access.
For broader sharing, consider Signed URLs for individual objects and IAM with allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers for public bucket-level access — but never combine public access with sensitive data.

question.title: Cloud Storage Consistency
question.scenario: An application uploads an object to Cloud Storage and immediately tries to read it.
question.question-text: What consistency does Cloud Storage provide for object operations?

choices.choice: Strong global consistency for all operations
Eventual consistency for reads after writes
Strong consistency only within the same region

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Storage delivers strong global consistency for all data and metadata operations. Once a write (upload, overwrite, or delete) returns success, every subsequent read from any location will see the result. This applies to object data, metadata, ACLs, and even bucket listing operations. There is no eventual consistency window. This simplifies application logic compared to storage systems that offer only eventual or read-your-writes consistency, because developers never need to handle stale reads or implement retry loops for consistency convergence.

ul.li: Bucket listing (list operations) is also strongly consistent: after a successful upload or delete, a subsequent list immediately reflects the change, with no lag or missing entries.
This strong consistency model was a significant engineering achievement for a globally distributed system and eliminates an entire class of race-condition bugs in distributed applications.

Object versioning does not weaken consistency: when versioning is enabled, overwriting an object immediately makes the new version the live version and the previous version a noncurrent version, both visible consistently.
Strong consistency applies regardless of bucket location type (regional, dual-regional, or multi-regional) and regardless of the storage class of the object.

question.title: Cloud Storage Versioning
question.scenario: A team needs to protect against accidental object deletion and maintain a history of all changes to objects.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Storage feature maintains previous versions of objects when they are overwritten or deleted?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The feature that preserves every historical version of an object — assigning each a unique generation number — so that overwrites and deletes create noncurrent versions instead of destroying data.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Object Versioning keeps a complete history of every object by retaining noncurrent versions when objects are overwritten or deleted. Each version gets a unique generation number, and deleted objects become noncurrent versions that can be restored by copying them back to the live version. Without lifecycle rules to prune old versions, versioned buckets accumulate storage costs for every historical version. Object holds prevent any deletion of specific objects. Retention policies enforce minimum retention durations. Soft delete is a separate feature that retains deleted objects for a configurable window but does not track overwrite history.

ul.li: Noncurrent versions incur the same per-GB storage charges as live objects; use lifecycle rules with a numNewerVersions or age condition to automatically delete old versions and control costs.
Object holds (event-based and temporary) prevent deletion of individual objects regardless of versioning or IAM permissions, useful for litigation holds on specific documents.
Retention policies set a minimum retention period at the bucket level and can be permanently locked via bucket lock; they prevent deletion but do not create version history.
Soft delete retains deleted objects for a configurable period (7-90 days) to protect against accidental deletion, but unlike versioning it does not preserve intermediate versions from overwrites.

question.title: Cloud Storage Encryption
question.scenario: A financial services company requires that they manage the encryption keys for data stored in Cloud Storage.
question.question-text: Which encryption option allows customers to control encryption keys stored in Cloud KMS?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: CMEK uses encryption keys that you create and manage in Cloud KMS, giving you control over key rotation, access policies, and the ability to revoke access by disabling a key.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) let you create and manage encryption keys in Cloud Key Management Service (KMS). You control key rotation schedules, set IAM policies on keys, and can revoke data access entirely by disabling or destroying the key. Google-managed keys provide default encryption but give you no control over key lifecycle. Customer-supplied keys (CSEK) require you to provide the raw key with every API request and Google never stores it. Client-side encryption happens before data reaches Google, shifting all key management to your application.

ul.li: CMEK keys can reside in Cloud KMS (software-backed), Cloud HSM (FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware), or Cloud External Key Manager (EKM) for keys held outside Google infrastructure entirely.
CSEK keys are never stored by Google — they must be provided as a Base64-encoded AES-256 key with every read or write request, making key loss equivalent to permanent data loss.
All Cloud Storage data is encrypted at rest by default using Google-managed keys with AES-256; CMEK and CSEK add customer control on top of this baseline encryption.

Cloud Audit Logs record every use of a CMEK key, providing an audit trail for compliance; disabling a CMEK key immediately renders all objects encrypted with it unreadable until the key is re-enabled.

question.title: Cloud Storage Bucket Location
question.scenario: A company needs to store data that will be accessed primarily from a single region to minimize latency and cost.
question.question-text: What type of Cloud Storage bucket location provides the lowest cost for single-region access?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Regional buckets store data redundantly within a single geographic region, offering the lowest storage cost per GB and the lowest latency for applications in that region. Multi-regional buckets replicate data across multiple regions in a continent for higher availability but cost more. Dual-regional buckets provide geo-redundancy between two specific regions at a premium. There is no "global bucket" location type in Cloud Storage. For single-region access patterns, the regional bucket is the most cost-effective and lowest-latency choice.

ul.li: Regional buckets still provide 99.999999999% (11 nines) annual durability through redundant storage across multiple zones within the region, so durability is not sacrificed for cost savings.
Dual-regional buckets store data in two specific regions you choose (e.g., us-east1 and us-west1), providing automatic failover and turbo replication with an RPO target of 15 minutes.
Multi-regional locations (US, EU, ASIA) distribute data across multiple regions within a continent, offering the highest availability but at the highest storage cost per GB.
Bucket location is permanent and cannot be changed after creation; choosing the wrong location requires creating a new bucket and migrating data with Storage Transfer Service or gsutil.

question.title: Cloud Storage Retention Policy
question.scenario: A company must comply with regulations requiring that certain data cannot be deleted for 7 years, even by administrators.
question.question-text: Which Cloud Storage feature prevents object deletion until a specified retention period has passed?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A retention policy sets a minimum retention duration on a bucket, and locking the bucket makes that policy permanent and irreversible — even project owners cannot delete objects before the period expires.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Retention policies define a minimum duration that every object in a bucket must be retained. When combined with bucket lock, the retention policy becomes permanent and cannot be removed, shortened, or overridden. This creates immutable storage meeting regulatory compliance requirements like WORM (Write Once Read Many). Even project owners and organization admins cannot delete locked objects before retention expires. IAM deny policies can be changed by sufficiently privileged admins. Object versioning preserves history but does not prevent deletion. Lifecycle rules automate deletion, the opposite of retention.

ul.li: Bucket lock is irreversible — once applied, the retention policy cannot be removed or shortened for the lifetime of the bucket, so thorough testing is essential before locking.
Object holds (event-based and temporary) provide additional per-object protection layered on top of retention policies, useful for litigation holds on specific documents within a retained bucket.

Retention policies prevent object deletion and overwrite but do not prevent reading; locked data remains accessible for the full retention period, satisfying both preservation and access requirements.
Lifecycle Delete rules cannot override a retention policy — if a lifecycle rule tries to delete an object still under retention, the deletion is silently skipped until the retention period expires.

question.title: Storage Transfer Service
question.scenario: A company needs to migrate 100 TB of data from AWS S3 to Cloud Storage with minimal manual effort.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides managed data transfer from other cloud providers to Cloud Storage?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Focus on the fully managed GCP service designed specifically for large-scale online data transfers from cloud sources like AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, and HTTP endpoints into Cloud Storage.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Storage Transfer Service is a managed, serverless service for transferring large volumes of data from online sources — including AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, other Cloud Storage buckets, and HTTP/HTTPS endpoints — into Cloud Storage. It handles scheduling, filtering, integrity verification, and automatic retries. Transfer Appliance is a physical device for offline transfer of datasets too large for network transfer. gsutil is a command-line tool suitable for smaller or scripted transfers but lacks the managed scheduling and scale of Storage Transfer Service. Dataflow is a data processing engine, not a storage migration tool.

ul.li: Transfer Appliance is for offline, physical data shipment — useful when network bandwidth is insufficient (e.g., transferring hundreds of TB over a slow link), but it takes days for shipping and handling.
Storage Transfer Service for on-premises data requires installing transfer agents on local machines to facilitate the transfer over the network into Cloud Storage.

gsutil rsync can transfer and synchronize data but runs on a single machine; for 100 TB it would take far longer and requires manual monitoring, unlike the fully managed parallel transfers of Storage Transfer Service.
Storage Transfer Service supports transfer manifests, bandwidth limits, and prefix/suffix filters to control exactly which objects are migrated, enabling incremental and selective migrations.

question.title: Persistent Disk Overview
question.scenario: A virtual machine needs reliable block storage for its operating system and application data.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides block storage for Compute Engine virtual machines?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for the network-attached block storage service whose data persists independently of the VM lifecycle and supports snapshots, resizing, and cross-zone replication.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Persistent Disk is Google Cloud's durable, network-attached block storage for Compute Engine VMs and GKE nodes. Data on a Persistent Disk persists independently of the VM: stopping or deleting a VM does not destroy the disk. It supports incremental snapshots for backup, online resizing without downtime, and automatic replication within the zone for durability. Cloud Storage is object storage accessed via HTTP, not block-level I/O. Filestore provides NFS file shares. Local SSD offers high-performance ephemeral storage that is lost when the VM stops.

ul.li: Persistent Disks can be attached to multiple VMs simultaneously in read-only mode, enabling shared boot images or configuration data across a fleet of instances.
Local SSD provides the lowest latency (sub-100 microsecond) and highest IOPS but data is ephemeral — it is lost on VM stop, termination, preemption, or host maintenance migration.
Cloud Storage is object storage (HTTP GET/PUT) not block storage (SCSI/NVMe), so it cannot serve as a boot disk or be mounted as a raw block device without an adapter like FUSE.
Persistent Disk types include Standard (HDD-backed), Balanced, SSD, and Extreme, each trading cost for IOPS and throughput to match different workload requirements.

question.title: Persistent Disk Types
question.scenario: A database workload requires the highest possible IOPS and throughput from block storage.
question.question-text: Which Persistent Disk type provides the highest performance for demanding workloads?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Extreme Persistent Disk delivers the highest performance among Persistent Disk types, with independently configurable IOPS (up to 120,000) and throughput decoupled from disk size. It is designed for enterprise databases like Oracle, SAP HANA, and SQL Server that demand predictable, high I/O. SSD Persistent Disk and Balanced Persistent Disk offer strong performance at lower cost but scale IOPS proportionally with size. Standard Persistent Disk is HDD-backed, offering the lowest cost but also the lowest performance.

ul.li: Extreme PD allows provisioning IOPS and throughput independently of disk capacity, so you can attach a small high-IOPS disk to a database VM without paying for unneeded storage.
Hyperdisk Extreme offers even higher IOPS limits (up to 350,000) and dynamic performance adjustment for specific machine types (e.g., C3, M3), surpassing traditional Extreme PD.
Balanced Persistent Disk provides SSD-class performance at a price point between Standard and SSD PD, making it the default choice for general-purpose workloads that do not need extreme IOPS.
Standard Persistent Disk uses HDD backing and is best suited for bulk storage, sequential I/O, and non-latency-sensitive workloads like log processing or large dataset storage.

question.title: Persistent Disk Snapshots
question.scenario: A company needs to create backups of their Persistent Disks that can be used to restore data or create new disks in any region.
question.question-text: Which feature creates point-in-time copies of Persistent Disks that can be stored across regions?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Snapshots create incremental, point-in-time backups of Persistent Disks. After the initial full snapshot, subsequent snapshots capture only changed blocks, reducing storage cost and creation time. Snapshots can be stored in multi-regional or regional locations and used to create new disks in any region, making them ideal for cross-region disaster recovery and migration. Object versioning applies to Cloud Storage, not block storage. Machine images capture entire VM configurations. Disk clones create instant copies but only within the same zone.

ul.li: Snapshots are incremental at the block level: only blocks changed since the last snapshot are stored, but each snapshot is independently restorable — deleting an intermediate snapshot does not break the chain.
Application-consistent snapshots require coordinating with the application (e.g., flushing database buffers, freezing the file system) before taking the snapshot to ensure data integrity.
Snapshot schedules can be attached to disks to automate regular backups with configurable retention policies (number of snapshots to keep or maximum age).
Disk clones use copy-on-write semantics for near-instant creation, but they are limited to the same zone as the source disk and cannot be used for cross-region recovery.

question.title: Local SSD
question.scenario: An application requires extremely low-latency storage for temporary data processing, and data loss on VM termination is acceptable.
question.question-text: Which storage option provides the lowest latency for Compute Engine VMs but does not persist data if the VM stops?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Local SSD provides high-performance storage physically attached to the server hosting your VM, offering sub-millisecond latency and very high IOPS via NVMe interface. However, data is ephemeral — it is lost when the VM stops, is deleted, is preempted, or undergoes a host maintenance event that requires migration to a new host. This makes it ideal for scratch space, caches, temporary processing buffers, and shuffle storage. Persistent Disk SSD and Balanced PD persist data across VM lifecycle events but have higher latency due to network attachment. RAM disk is not a GCP storage product.

ul.li: Local SSDs come in fixed 375 GB partitions; you can attach up to 24 partitions (9 TB total) per VM, depending on the machine type, and they can be configured as a single RAID-0 array.
Local SSD data survives live migration events (where the VM moves to another host without stopping), but does not survive VM stop, restart, termination, or preemption.
Persistent Disk (SSD or Balanced) should be used for any data that must survive VM lifecycle events — OS boot disks, application data, and databases all require persistent storage.
Local SSD pricing is included in the VM cost for certain machine types (e.g., C3-lssd) or billed per-partition-hour for standard machine types, with no charge for I/O operations.

question.title: Filestore Overview
question.scenario: An application requires shared file storage accessible by multiple VMs simultaneously using standard file system protocols.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides managed NFS file shares for Compute Engine and GKE?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider the specific requirements and constraints in the scenario to determine which option best addresses all of them.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Filestore is a fully managed network file storage service that exposes NFSv3 file shares. Multiple Compute Engine VMs and GKE pods can mount the same Filestore instance simultaneously with full read-write access, making it suitable for shared configuration, content management, media processing, and legacy applications that require POSIX file system semantics. Cloud Storage FUSE mounts object storage as a file system but with different performance and consistency characteristics. Cloud Storage is object storage without native mount capability. Persistent Disk supports multi-attach only in read-only mode.

ul.li: Filestore tiers include Basic (HDD and SSD for development and small workloads), Zonal (high performance within a single zone), and Enterprise (multi-zonal replication with 99.99% SLA).
Cloud Storage FUSE allows mounting Cloud Storage buckets as directories, but it is not POSIX-compliant, has higher latency for metadata operations, and does not support file locking.
Persistent Disk multi-attach supports connecting a single disk to multiple VMs but only in read-only mode, making it unsuitable for shared read-write file workloads.
Filestore integrates with GKE via the CSI driver, allowing dynamic provisioning of NFS volumes as PersistentVolumeClaims in Kubernetes workloads.

question.title: Filestore Tiers
question.scenario: A media company needs high-performance shared storage that can survive a zone failure without data loss.
question.question-text: Which Filestore tier provides multi-zonal availability for high availability requirements?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Filestore Enterprise tier provides regional availability by replicating data synchronously across multiple zones in the same region. It offers a 99.99% availability SLA and is designed for business-critical workloads that must tolerate zone failures. The Zonal tier provides high performance within a single zone but cannot survive a zone outage. Basic HDD and Basic SSD tiers are single-zone without built-in redundancy and offer no high-availability guarantees beyond local disk durability.

ul.li: Enterprise tier requires a minimum capacity of 1 TB and can scale up to 10 TB; it supports both NFS and snapshot capabilities for backup and point-in-time recovery.
Zonal tier offers the best price-performance ratio for high-throughput workloads (e.g., rendering, genomics) that can tolerate single-zone placement or handle zone failure at the application layer.
Basic tiers (HDD and SSD) are the most cost-effective options for development, testing, and small production workloads that do not require high availability or high throughput.
Enterprise tier supports automated backups and can be used with GKE's CSI driver for dynamically provisioned, highly available shared volumes in Kubernetes clusters.

question.title: Hyperdisk
question.scenario: A database workload needs the ability to dynamically change IOPS and throughput without recreating the disk.
question.question-text: Which storage option allows provisioning IOPS and throughput independently and changing them dynamically?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Hyperdisk lets you provision disk capacity, IOPS, and throughput as independent dimensions and adjust any of them dynamically without recreating the disk or detaching it from the VM. This gives you the flexibility to right-size performance for current workload demands and scale up or down as needs change. Local SSD performance is fixed by the hardware. Persistent Disk SSD and Balanced PD scale performance proportionally with disk size, so increasing IOPS requires increasing capacity even if more storage is not needed.

ul.li: Hyperdisk comes in three types: Extreme (highest IOPS, up to 350,000), Throughput (optimized for high sequential bandwidth), and Balanced (general-purpose with moderate IOPS and throughput).

Traditional Persistent Disk types tie performance to size — for example, SSD PD provides 30 IOPS per GB, so reaching 30,000 IOPS requires provisioning at least 1 TB, even if the workload needs only 100 GB of capacity.
Hyperdisk supports dynamic performance changes via the gcloud CLI or API; adjustments take effect within minutes and do not require VM restart or disk detach/reattach.
Hyperdisk is available only on specific machine types (C3, M3, and later series); check compatibility with your chosen machine type before planning a migration from Persistent Disk.

question.title: Regional Persistent Disk
question.scenario: A company needs block storage that can survive a zone failure and allow the VM to be restarted in another zone using the same data.
question.question-text: Which Persistent Disk configuration provides synchronous replication across two zones?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Regional Persistent Disk synchronously replicates block data to two zones within a region. If the active zone fails, you can force-attach the disk to a VM in the secondary zone with near-zero RPO (recovery point objective). This provides significantly better availability than zonal disks. Multi-attach PD shares a single disk across VMs but does not replicate data. Snapshots and scheduled backups have RPO measured in hours and require restore time. Regional PD costs approximately double a comparable zonal PD because you pay for storage in both zones.

ul.li: Regional Persistent Disk provides a 99.99% availability SLA compared to 99.9% for zonal Persistent Disk, a 10x improvement in expected annual downtime minutes.
During a zone failure, you must use the force-attach API to reassign the disk to a VM in the surviving zone; this is a manual or automation-triggered step, not automatic failover.
Synchronous replication introduces slightly higher write latency (typically a few hundred microseconds) compared to zonal PD because every write must be acknowledged by both zone replicas.
Regional PD can be combined with managed instance groups (MIGs) and autohealing to build self-recovering applications that automatically restart in the healthy zone during a zonal outage.

question.title: Cloud Storage FUSE
question.scenario: An application needs to access Cloud Storage objects using standard file system commands without code changes.
question.question-text: Which tool mounts Cloud Storage buckets as local file systems on Compute Engine VMs?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the access patterns, durability needs, and performance characteristics the scenario requires from its storage layer.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Storage FUSE is an open-source adapter that mounts Cloud Storage buckets as local file system directories on Linux VMs. Applications can use standard POSIX file I/O operations (open, read, write, close) to interact with objects in the bucket without any code modifications. However, FUSE has different performance and consistency characteristics than a native file system. Storage Transfer Service migrates data between storage systems, not mount them. gsutil is a CLI tool for copying objects, not for mounting. Filestore is a separate managed NFS service, not a Cloud Storage adapter.

ul.li: Cloud Storage FUSE is not fully POSIX-compliant: operations like atomic rename, hard links, and file locking are not supported, which can break applications that depend on these semantics.
Metadata operations (stat, list directory) have significantly higher latency than a local file system because each operation requires an HTTP round trip to the Cloud Storage API.
FUSE performs best with large sequential reads and writes (e.g., reading training data for ML workloads); small random I/O patterns suffer from the per-operation HTTP overhead.

For workloads needing POSIX compliance, file locking, and low-latency metadata operations, Filestore (managed NFS) is a better choice, though it does not offer Cloud Storage's global accessibility or storage-class tiering.

question.title: Backup and DR for Compute Engine
question.scenario: A company needs an enterprise-grade backup solution for their Compute Engine VMs that provides centralized management and compliance reporting.
question.question-text: Which Google Cloud service provides managed backup and disaster recovery for Compute Engine?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider what recovery guarantees the scenario needs and which approach provides them with the least operational overhead.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Google Cloud Backup and DR Service is a fully managed backup and disaster recovery platform that provides centralized policy management, application-consistent backups for enterprise databases, incremental-forever backup with instant mount recovery, and built-in compliance reporting and SLA monitoring. Snapshot schedules provide basic automated disk-level backups but lack application awareness, centralized management, and compliance features. Cloud Storage transfer moves object data and is not a backup solution. VM cloning creates a one-time copy without ongoing backup capability.

ul.li: Backup and DR Service supports application-aware backups for databases including Oracle, SQL Server, SAP HANA, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, ensuring transactional consistency at backup time.
Instant mount recovery allows mounting a backup directly as a disk on a new VM, enabling rapid recovery without waiting for a full data restore — critical for meeting tight RTO targets.
The service provides centralized dashboards for backup job monitoring, SLA compliance tracking, and audit logging, meeting enterprise governance requirements that basic snapshots cannot address.

Incremental-forever backups capture only changed blocks after the initial full backup, minimizing storage consumption and backup window duration while maintaining the ability to restore to any point in time.

question.title: Database Selection: Web Application
question.scenario: A new e-commerce startup needs a database for their web application. They require a relational database with standard SQL support, and their users are primarily in one geographic region.
question.question-text: Which database service is most appropriate for a regional e-commerce application needing standard SQL?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For a regional e-commerce app that needs familiar relational SQL with manageable cost, consider the fully managed service offering MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud SQL is the best fit for a regional e-commerce startup requiring standard SQL. It provides managed MySQL or PostgreSQL with familiar tooling, automated backups and patching, high availability within a region, and cost-effective pricing for single-region workloads. Cloud Spanner provides global scale but at much higher cost — overkill for a regional startup. Firestore is a NoSQL document database without SQL join support. Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store designed for analytics and time-series, not transactional e-commerce workflows.

ul.li: Cloud SQL supports up to 64 TB of storage per instance and handles most transactional e-commerce workloads (product catalogs, orders, user accounts) without architectural complexity.
When the startup outgrows Cloud SQL's single-region or single-write-primary limits, Cloud Spanner provides a horizontal scaling upgrade path with SQL compatibility.

Firestore is better suited for mobile apps needing offline sync and real-time updates; its document model does not support relational joins required for complex e-commerce queries like order-product-customer reports.
Bigtable lacks SQL support, secondary indexes, and multi-row transactions — essential features for e-commerce operations like cart checkout that span multiple table rows atomically.

question.title: Database Selection: Global Gaming
question.scenario: A gaming company needs a database for player profiles and game state that provides low-latency access globally and strong consistency for in-game transactions.
question.question-text: Which database best serves a globally distributed gaming application requiring strong consistency?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: For a globally distributed game requiring strong consistency and SQL transactions across continents, the only GCP database with external consistency and horizontal scaling is the right choice.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Spanner is ideal for globally distributed gaming because it provides SQL support, automatic sharding, multi-region replication with strong (external) consistency, and the ability to handle high-throughput transactions across continents without consistency compromises. Gaming workloads like player inventory, matchmaking, and leaderboards benefit from globally atomic transactions. Memorystore is an in-memory cache limited to a single region. Firestore offers global availability but has different consistency semantics and lacks SQL joins. Cloud SQL with read replicas provides asynchronous replication that cannot guarantee strong consistency across regions.

ul.li: Spanner's TrueTime mechanism — using atomic clocks and GPS receivers in every data center — enables globally consistent transactions with externally valid timestamps, critical for preventing item duplication or currency exploits in games.
Multi-region Spanner configurations provide 99.999% availability (about 5 minutes of downtime per year), exceeding the uptime requirements of most real-time multiplayer games.

Firestore offers global access and strong consistency for individual document reads but does not support SQL joins or complex cross-document queries needed for relational game state like inventory-to-player lookups.

Cloud SQL read replicas use asynchronous replication, so a player's recent action on one continent might not be visible to another player on a different continent for seconds — unacceptable for real-time competitive games.

question.title: Database Selection: Mobile App
question.scenario: A team is building a mobile app that needs offline support, real-time sync between devices, and the ability to scale from zero users during development to millions in production.
question.question-text: Which database is best suited for a mobile application with offline and real-time sync requirements?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The serverless document database with native mobile SDKs, built-in offline persistence, real-time listeners, and pay-per-operation pricing that scales to zero is the natural fit for mobile apps.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Firestore is purpose-built for mobile and web applications. Its client SDKs provide offline persistence (caching data locally so the app works without connectivity), real-time listeners (pushing changes instantly to all connected devices), and automatic scaling from zero to millions of users with pay-per-operation pricing.
